title: Hormonal Regulation of Metabolism
objectives: Identify key metabolic hormones and their primary target tissues
Explain insulin/glucagon signaling pathways and their opposing effects
Describe hormonal adaptations to fed vs. fasted states
Recognize endocrine disorders of metabolic regulation

major_hormones.title: Key Metabolic Hormones
major_hormones.content:
• Insulin (β-cells) - Fed state regulator
  • Glucagon (α-cells) - Fasted state activator
  • Cortisol - Stress-induced catabolism
  • Leptin - Adipose-derived satiety signal
  • Adiponectin - Insulin sensitizer

insulin_glucagon.title: Insulin vs. Glucagon Signaling
insulin_glucagon.content:
Insulin Pathway
• Receptor: Tyrosine kinase
• Key action: ↑GLUT4 translocation
• Metabolic effects:
- ↑Glycogen synthesis
- ↑Lipogenesis
- ↓Gluconeogenesis
Glucagon Pathway
• Receptor: GPCR (Gs-coupled)
• Key action: ↑cAMP → PKA activation
• Metabolic effects:
- ↑Glycogenolysis
- ↑Gluconeogenesis
- ↑Lipolysis

fed_fasted.title: Fed vs. Fasted State Transitions
fed_fasted.content:
Postprandial (Fed) State

  • ↑Insulin/↓Glucagon ratio
  • Glucose → Glycogen (liver/muscle)
  • Excess glucose → Fatty acids (liver → adipose)

Fasted State (>12h)

  • ↓Insulin/↑Glucagon ratio
  • Glycogen → Glucose (first 24h)
  • Proteolysis → Gluconeogenesis (>24h)
  • Lipolysis → Ketones (>48h)

stress_hormones.title: Stress Hormones & Counter-Regulation
stress_hormones.content:
Cortisol
• Action: ↑Gluconeogenesis (PEPCK activation)
• Effect: Hyperglycemia
• Clinical: Dawn phenomenon
Epinephrine
• Action: ↑Glycogenolysis (muscle/liver)
• Effect: Rapid glucose mobilization
• Clinical: Fight-or-flight response

clinical_relevance.title: Endocrine Disorders
clinical_relevance.content:
Type 1 Diabetes Mellitus

Cause: Autoimmune β-cell destruction

Lab Findings: ↑Glucose, ↑Ketones, ↓Insulin/C-peptide

Treatment: Insulin replacement

Metabolic Syndrome

Features: Insulin resistance + 3 of:
- Central obesity
- Hypertension
- Dyslipidemia
- Fasting hyperglycemia

Mechanism: Leptin/adiponectin imbalance

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Why does cortisol cause both fat redistribution and muscle wasting?

Cortisol activates lipoprotein lipase in central adipocytes (truncal fat accumulation) while simultaneously triggering muscle proteolysis to provide gluconeogenic substrates (alanine/glutamine).

How does leptin resistance develop in obesity?

Chronic hyperleptinemia downregulates hypothalamic leptin receptors and SOCS3 signaling, creating a threshold shift requiring higher leptin levels for satiety effects.

Why do β-blockers mask hypoglycemia symptoms?

By antagonizing adrenergic receptors, they blunt epinephrine-mediated warning signs (tachycardia, tremors) while preserving neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, seizures).
